newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. demands Israel halt construction in E.Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: U.N. demands Israel halt construction in E.Jerusalem.

text.p: An emergency special session of the General Assembly demanded on Friday an immediate halt to the construction of an Israeli settlement in East Jerusalem and called for an end to all assistance to "illegal Israeli activities" in the occupied territories.
The vote was 134 to three, with 11 abstentions. Voting against were the United States, Israel and Micronesia.

Abstaining were: Australia, Canada, Germany, Latvia, Liberia, Lithuania, Marshall Islands, Norway, Romania, Rwanda and Uruguay. By abstaining, Germany broke ranks with its other European Union partners.

The special session was the fourth time a U.N. body debated an Israeli decision last month to build 6,500 homes for Jews at a site, called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic, captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
Virtually all speakers criticised Israel's action. Most of those who abstained felt the resolution would not help the Middle East peace process.

The session, requested by the Arab group of states spearheaded by the Palestine Liberation Organisation, marked only the 10th time the assembly had met under a 1950 procedure allowing an issue considered a threat to peace to be transferred to the assembly if a veto prevents the 15-nation Security Council from taking action.
There is no veto in the 185-member assembly, whose decisions are not binding.

The United States used its veto March 7 and March 21 to block council resolutions calling on Israel not to proceed with the housing project, which sparked Palestinian protests and further clouded the Middle East peace process.
While critical of the Israeli building project, the United States said differences between Israel and the Palestinians should be settled in bilateral negotiations.

On March 13, a non-emergency session of the assembly voted 130 to two (U.S. and Israel), with two abstentions (Marshall Islands and Micronesia), for a resolution calling on Israel to abandon its construction plan.

The latest resolution, tougher and more detailed than those debated last month, "condemns the construction by Israel, the occupying power, of a new settlement in Jabal Abu Ghneim ... and all other illegal Israeli actions in all the occupied territories."
It demands "immediate and full cessation of the construction ... and of all other Israeli settlement activities."

In an approach to sanctions, which only the Security Council can impose, the resolution calls for "the cessation of all forms of assistance and support for illegal Israeli activities" in the occupied territories, particularly settlement activities.

An earlier version, softened to gain the support of Western countries, would have recommended that all states bar any assistance, trade or financial dealings with Israeli private or public bodies involved in settlement activities.

The adopted resolution recommends that the parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits settlements in occupied territories, "take measures, on a national or regional level ... to ensure respect by Israel" for it.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan is asked to "monitor the situation and to submit a report" within two months.

Another provision recommends that a just and lasting solution to the question of Jerusalem should include "internationally guaranteed provisions to ensure the freedom of religion and of conscience of its inhabitants" as well as "permanent, free and unhindered access to the Holy Places by the faithful of all religions and nationalities."
A paragraph included at the urging of some Western states, "rejects terrorism in all its forms and manifestations."

The emergency special session was adjourned "temporarily" but authorised to resume at the request of member states. A 1980 special session on the question of Palestine was resumed four times during 1982.
